requirements.given: Marketing offer is displayed as '0% APR for 18 months' in large text, with deferred-interest retroactive-charge terms only in small print/footnote.
requirements.when: Evaluate whether the overall net impression a reasonable consumer would form matches the actual mechanics the interest engine implements.
requirements.then: prominence and clarity of the retroactive-interest risk is proportionate — not so buried that the net impression is deceptive — and matches actual system behavior exactly.
requirements.failureMode: system's actual retroactive-charge behavior is harsher than what a reasonable reading of the offer would lead a consumer to expect (e.g., charges interest on the ORIGINAL balance even after partial payment, but the offer implies only the remaining balance is at risk).
requirements.blockedOn: promo periods with start and end dates

requirements.title: Rate/fee change is never applied silently without required notice
requirements.given: A discretionary APR increase is scheduled to take effect.
requirements.when: Verify the increase cannot take effect in the system if the required 45-day notice was not actually generated and delivered (not just logged as 'intended to send').
requirements.then: rate-change effective-date logic is hard-linked to confirmed notice delivery, not just an internal flag that could be set without the notice actually going out.
requirements.failureMode: notice-sent flag can be set (e.g., by a batch job bug) without the actual notice being delivered, letting the rate increase take effect while the customer was never actually informed — both a Reg Z and an unfair-practice issue.

requirements.title: Payment allocation doesn't default to the option that maximizes issuer revenue when a customer choice is required
requirements.given: Reg Z lets issuers apply CARD Act allocation rules by default, but if the system offers customers an allocation choice, that choice must be honored.
requirements.when: Customer selects a specific payment-allocation preference where the system offers one; verify the system actually applies the selected preference rather than silently reverting to whichever allocation generates more interest.
requirements.then: customer's selected preference is honored on every subsequent payment until changed.
requirements.failureMode: system accepts the customer's selection in the UI but the payment-processing backend ignores it and applies the default/legally-minimum allocation instead — a dark-pattern-adjacent bug.

requirements.title: Add-on product enrollment doesn't silently change effective APR/finance charges
requirements.given: Customer is offered an optional payment-protection or credit-monitoring add-on during a service call or online flow.
requirements.when: Simulate an ambiguous or rushed consent flow and check whether enrollment can complete without clear, affirmative, informed consent.
requirements.then: enrollment requires unambiguous affirmative consent with the cost and its effect on the account's finance charges clearly disclosed before completion; no pre-checked boxes or silent enrollment.
requirements.failureMode: system allows enrollment via a pre-checked default or a single ambiguous click, and the add-on fee subsequently increases the account's effective finance charge without a clear, separate disclosure of that impact.
requirements.blockedOn: account lifecycle dates and product conversion

requirements.title: Charged-off account interest/fee practices remain accurate, not just aggressive
requirements.given: Account is charged off after prolonged delinquency; collections activity continues.
requirements.when: Verify what interest/fees, if any, continue to accrue post-charge-off and whether that matches what's disclosed to the customer in collections communications.
requirements.then: any continued interest/fee accrual exactly matches the account's actual legal terms and is accurately represented in every collections communication.
requirements.failureMode: collections communications state one balance/rate while the system's internal ledger is actually accruing a different (often higher, uncommunicated) amount — creating a discrepancy between what the customer is told they owe and what the system will actually try to collect.
requirements.blockedOn: account lifecycle dates and product conversion

requirements.title: System cannot apply a rate/fee that contradicts the customer's actual accepted terms version
requirements.given: Cardholder agreement has been amended over time (v1 at account opening, v2 after a disclosed change); customer never affirmatively accepted v2 in a context requiring opt-in (e.g., a change requiring assent, not just notice).
requirements.when: Verify the rate/fee engine is applying the terms version the customer actually agreed to, tracked with an effective-date-versioned terms record.
requirements.then: system correctly ties each account to the specific, current, properly-noticed/accepted version of terms and can produce that record on demand.
requirements.failureMode: system has a single 'current terms' global config, unable to prove which version a given customer actually agreed to or was properly noticed of, at the time a disputed charge occurred.

requirements.title: Marketing-stated 'no annual fee' claim matches actual fee configuration
requirements.given: Product is marketed as having no annual fee.
requirements.when: Verify no annual-fee line item can be generated for that product code under any account configuration path (including manual overrides).
requirements.then: fee engine has a hard product-level constraint preventing an annual fee from ever being assessed on that product code.
requirements.failureMode: a manual override or a misconfigured account migration can still cause an annual fee to post on a 'no annual fee' product, contradicting the marketed claim.
requirements.blockedOn: override expiry dates and authorisation records

requirements.title: Auto-enrollment or auto-renewal into a new promo doesn't extend obligations without consent
requirements.given: A promotional rate is expiring; system offers an 'auto-renew into a new 12-month promo' feature.
requirements.when: Verify the renewal requires an affirmative action, not silent continuation, if it materially changes the customer's terms (e.g., a new deferred-interest period with retroactive-charge risk).
requirements.then: renewal into a materially different obligation requires clear affirmative consent, not a default opt-in.
requirements.failureMode: system auto-enrolls the customer into a new deferred-interest promo period (resetting retroactive-interest risk) without any affirmative action, simply because they didn't opt out in time.
requirements.blockedOn: promo periods with start and end dates

requirements.title: 21-day rule: statement delivered at least 21 days before due date
requirements.given: Statement is generated and the due date is calculated.
requirements.when: Measure the actual gap between statement mailing/delivery date and the payment due date across several cycles, including short months.
requirements.then: gap is always at least 21 days; if a scheduling bug would produce a shorter window, the system extends the due date rather than shortening the notice period.
requirements.failureMode: a short month or holiday-adjusted mailing schedule compresses the gap below 21 days, and the system charges a late fee or starts the delinquency clock anyway on a payment that was technically on time under the 21-day rule.

requirements.title: Over-limit fees/interest require affirmative opt-in
requirements.given: Customer has NOT opted in to over-limit transaction processing.
requirements.when: Simulate a transaction that would push the balance over the credit limit.
requirements.then: transaction is declined (or approved with no over-limit fee/interest consequence), since the customer never opted in.
requirements.failureMode: system approves the over-limit transaction and assesses an over-limit fee or elevated interest despite no opt-in on file.

requirements.title: Fixed, consistent monthly due date
requirements.given: Account's due date is set to the 15th of each month.
requirements.when: Verify the due date across several cycles including February and 31-day months.
requirements.then: due date remains the 15th every cycle (a genuinely fixed date), not silently drifting due to a 'same weekday' or 'X days after statement' miscalculation.
requirements.failureMode: due-date calculation logic actually computes 'statement date + 21 days' each cycle, causing the due date to drift by a few days month to month despite being disclosed as a fixed date.

requirements.title: Late fees stay within Reg Z safe-harbor caps
requirements.given: A late payment triggers a late fee assessment. Compare the assessed fee against the current Reg Z 1026.52 safe-harbor maximum (and the account's own minimum-payment-based proportionality where applicable) for a first vs.
requirements.when: subsequent late payment within 6 billing cycles.
requirements.then: fee is at or below the applicable safe-harbor cap, and correctly distinguishes first-offense vs. repeat-offense caps within the 6-cycle window.
requirements.failureMode: fee schedule is a flat hardcoded value that either exceeds the current safe-harbor cap (stale config after a regulatory cap change) or fails to apply the lower first-offense cap.

requirements.title: No two-cycle (double-cycle) billing method
requirements.given: Customer carried a balance in the prior cycle and pays it in full during the current cycle, then makes a new purchase.
requirements.when: Verify the balance computation method used for interest never reaches back into the prior, already-closed billing cycle's balance.
requirements.then: interest is computed using only the current cycle's balance data (e.g., average daily balance for the current cycle), consistent with CARD Act's ban on double-cycle billing.
requirements.failureMode: legacy balance-computation code path still references the previous cycle's ending balance when computing current-cycle interest — a double-cycle billing method CARD Act specifically outlawed.

requirements.title: Credit line increase requires ability-to-pay reassessment
requirements.given: System (or a CSR) initiates a credit-limit increase on an existing account.
requirements.when: Verify an ability-to-pay check is performed and documented before the increase takes effect, consistent with the same requirement applied at account opening.
requirements.then: increase is blocked until a current ability-to-pay assessment is completed and passes.
requirements.failureMode: credit-limit increases go through an operationally separate workflow that never re-checks ability-to-pay, only the original at account-opening check (now stale).
requirements.blockedOn: account lifecycle dates and product conversion

requirements.title: Minimum-payment warning box uses accurate total-interest and payoff-time projections
requirements.given: Statement's required minimum-payment warning box projects payoff time and total interest if only minimums are paid going forward.
requirements.when: Verify the projection engine uses the account's actual current APR(s) per balance bucket and a realistic minimum-payment formula (not a generic placeholder).
requirements.then: projected payoff time and total interest are computed correctly from live account data and reconcile with a manual recomputation within rounding tolerance.
requirements.failureMode: projection uses a single blended/default APR unrelated to the account's actual per-bucket rates, producing a materially wrong (often understated) total-interest projection.
requirements.blockedOn: product configuration and disclosed rate ranges

requirements.title: Under-21 cardholder rate-increase restrictions honored
requirements.given: Applicant is under 21 without an eligible co-signer/proof of independent income.
requirements.when: Verify account opening is blocked or restricted per CARD Act's under-21 protections, and that any later rate changes on such accounts follow the same heightened protections.
requirements.then: system enforces the under-21 opening restrictions and carries any associated protections through to subsequent rate-change logic.
requirements.failureMode: age-based restriction is checked only at the application stage and has no bearing on later automated rate-increase logic, allowing a protected young cardholder's rate to be increased in ways the Act restricts.
requirements.blockedOn: account lifecycle dates and product conversion

requirements.title: Minimum payment formula changes are disclosed and don't function as a disguised cost-increase
requirements.driver: JPMorgan Chase minimum-payment class action settlement (2012, ~$100M) — illustrative precedent, not itself an APR case
requirements.given: Issuer decides to raise the required minimum payment percentage of balance (e.g., from 2% to 5%) for existing accounts.
requirements.when: Verify this change goes through proper change-in-terms disclosure and isn't used as a mechanism to effectively accelerate cost/fees without the disclosure rigor applied to an actual APR increase.
requirements.then: minimum payment formula changes are clearly disclosed with adequate advance notice, and the system does not use minimum-payment changes as a substitute path to achieve what would otherwise require a disclosed rate increase.
requirements.failureMode: system changes the minimum-payment formula with materially weaker notice/disclosure than an APR change would require, even though the practical effect on cardholders (and issuer revenue from resulting fees/interest) is similar — echoing prior credit-card litigation over minimum-payment-formula changes.

requirements.title: Records retained for the required minimum period
requirements.given: An APR calculation dispute arises for a transaction that occurred 20 months ago.
requirements.when: Attempt to retrieve the full rate-calculation inputs (rate table version, balance snapshot, day-count) for that historical date.
requirements.then: complete records are retrievable for at least the Reg Z-required retention period (generally 2 years for compliance examination purposes), with correct historical versioning (not just the current rate table).
requirements.failureMode: system only retains the CURRENT rate table with no historical versioning, making it impossible to reconstruct what rate was actually in effect and used on a past date.
requirements.blockedOn: product configuration and disclosed rate ranges

requirements.title: Grace-period unavailability is disclosed when applicable
requirements.given: A product/account configuration has no grace period at all (interest accrues from transaction date even on full-payoff accounts) — a valid but less common configuration.
requirements.when: Check whether this is clearly and specifically disclosed to the customer, distinct from products that do offer a grace period.
requirements.then: absence of a grace period is affirmatively and clearly disclosed, not left implicit or inferred from silence in the disclosure document.
requirements.failureMode: same generic disclosure template is used for both grace-period and no-grace-period products, with the applicable-terms field simply left blank instead of an explicit statement.

requirements.title: Only enumerated Reg Z 1026.55 exceptions trigger a mid-term APR increase
requirements.given: A mid-term APR increase is applied to an existing balance outside the first 12 months.
requirements.when: For every mid-term increase the system ever applies, verify it maps to one of the specific enumerated Reg Z 1026.55(b) exceptions (index/formula change, workout-program completion or failure, 60+ days delinquent, or expiration of a previously disclosed temporary rate) with a logged reason code.
requirements.then: every mid-term increase has a valid, logged, enumerated reason code; increases with no valid mapped reason are blocked entirely.
requirements.failureMode: system allows a generic 'business decision' or unmapped reason code to trigger a mid-term increase on an existing balance, which Reg Z doesn't permit outside the enumerated exceptions.
requirements.blockedOn: override expiry dates and authorisation records

requirements.title: Temporary rate expiration exception requires the ORIGINAL disclosure to have stated the specific expiration terms
requirements.given: A promotional rate is expiring and reverting to standard APR under the 1026.55(b)(3) exception.
requirements.when: Verify the promo's original disclosure actually specified the length of the promo period and the specific post-expiration rate (or formula) at the time it was first offered.
requirements.then: reversion is only permitted because the original disclosure met the specific-terms requirement; if it didn't, the system should not treat this as a valid 1026.55 exception.
requirements.failureMode: system allows reversion to standard APR under the 'temporary rate expired' exception even when the original promo disclosure was vague about the post-expiration rate, which doesn't qualify for the exception.
requirements.blockedOn: promo periods with start and end dates

requirements.title: Workout/hardship program completion vs. failure both handled per their own disclosed terms
requirements.given: Customer enters a hardship workout program with a temporary reduced APR, contingent on completing a defined payment plan.
requirements.when: Simulate both a successful completion and a failure (missed payment) partway through the plan.
requirements.then: successful completion transitions the account per the disclosed post-program terms; failure reverts per the disclosed failure terms (which may differ) — both paths logged with the specific 1026.55(b)(2) basis.
requirements.failureMode: system has only a single 'workout ended' state with no distinction between successful completion and failure, applying the same (often wrong) reversion rate regardless of outcome.
requirements.blockedOn: override expiry dates and authorisation records

requirements.title: Balance-computation method matches what's disclosed, exactly
requirements.given: Account-opening disclosure states 'Average Daily Balance (including new purchases)' as the balance computation method.
requirements.when: Verify the actual interest-calculation code path matches this exact method, not a different valid-but-undisclosed method like 'Average Daily Balance (excluding new purchases)' or 'previous balance method.'.
requirements.then: calculation method used in production exactly matches the disclosed method, including whether new purchases are included in the averaging.
requirements.failureMode: a code refactor or product migration silently switches the balance-computation method (e.g., to exclude new purchases) without a corresponding disclosure update — same-sounding methods produce different dollar amounts.

requirements.title: Reg Z definitions applied consistently between disclosure and actual system logic for 'business day'
requirements.given: Multiple Reg Z provisions (21-day rule, weekend/holiday due-date handling, notice timing) depend on the definition of 'business day.'.
requirements.when: Verify a single, correctly Reg-Z-aligned definition of business day (generally, all calendar days except Sundays and specified federal holidays) is used consistently across every provision that depends on it.
requirements.then: one consistent business-day calendar/definition is used everywhere day-counting matters for compliance purposes.
requirements.failureMode: different subsystems use different business-day definitions (e.g., one excludes Saturdays, another doesn't), causing the SAME date to be compliant under one calculation and non-compliant under another for the exact same customer event.

requirements.title: Payoff quote precision matches actual accrual engine through the quoted date
requirements.given: Customer requests a payoff quote 'good through' a specific future date, 9 days from today.
requirements.when: Generate the payoff quote, then let those 9 days actually elapse with no other account activity, and compare the quoted amount to what the live accrual engine independently computes on the quoted date.
requirements.then: quoted amount matches the live-engine amount exactly (to the cent) — same day-count method, same rate, same rounding rule used by both systems.
requirements.failureMode: payoff-quote service is a separate codepath (often a simplified/legacy calculator) that uses a different divisor, rounding rule, or doesn't account for a rate that's about to change, so the customer who pays the exact quoted amount is left with a small residual balance or credit.
requirements.blockedOn: product configuration and disclosed rate ranges

requirements.title: Negative amortization when minimum payment is less than accruing interest
requirements.given: Account has a high APR (e.g., 29.99%) and a low credit limit, such that the disclosed minimum payment formula produces a minimum smaller than the interest accruing that cycle.
requirements.when: Make on-time minimum payments for several consecutive cycles with no new purchases.
requirements.then: system correctly recognizes and discloses that the balance is increasing despite on-time payments (negative amortization), and the minimum-payment-warning-box payoff projection reflects a balance that grows before it shrinks, or flags that minimum payments alone will never pay off the balance.
requirements.failureMode: minimum-payment-warning-box projection logic assumes payments always reduce principal, so it computes and discloses a finite payoff date/total-interest figure that is mathematically impossible given the actual rate and payment amount — a disclosure that's not just imprecise but wrong in direction.

requirements.title: Product conversion mid-cycle blends old and new product APR by day
requirements.given: Customer is upgraded from a standard product (18.99% APR) to a premium product (16.99% APR) on day 12 of a 30-day billing cycle.
requirements.when: Compute interest for that transition cycle.
requirements.then: interest is calculated as two correctly-bounded segments — days 1–12 at the old product's rate, days 13–30 at the new product's rate — summing correctly, the same way a mid-cycle prime-rate change is handled.
requirements.failureMode: system applies a single rate for the whole transition cycle (either the old or new rate, whichever the rate table happened to reflect when the batch job ran), overcharging or undercharging depending on direction.
requirements.blockedOn: account lifecycle dates and product conversion

requirements.title: Statement/due-date change produces a non-standard transition cycle with correct day-count
requirements.given: Customer requests (or issuer initiates) a due-date change from the 15th to the 1st, producing a one-time 16-day transition cycle instead of the usual ~30-day cycle.
requirements.when: Compute interest and average daily balance for the 16-day transition cycle.
requirements.then: day-count and ADB logic correctly use the actual 16 days of the transition cycle, not a hardcoded assumption of ~30 days.
requirements.failureMode: interest engine has a hardcoded or defaulted 'days in cycle' constant used for a sanity check or a shortcut calculation, silently miscalculating interest for any non-standard-length cycle.

requirements.title: Merchant-category (MCC) based differential APR bucket assignment
requirements.given: Card offers a promotional rate (or deferred interest) specific to purchases at a named retailer or merchant category, alongside standard-rate purchases elsewhere.
requirements.when: Make purchases at the qualifying MCC and at a non-qualifying MCC in the same cycle.
requirements.then: each transaction is assigned to the correct APR bucket based on its actual MCC at time of authorization, and interest accrues per-bucket correctly.
requirements.failureMode: mCC-based bucket assignment is evaluated at settlement rather than authorization (or vice versa, depending on what's disclosed), or a merchant's MCC changes/gets recoded between authorization and settlement, silently reclassifying a transaction into the wrong rate bucket with no reconciliation check.

requirements.title: Fee amounts are deliberately classified as interest-bearing or not, consistently
requirements.given: A late fee and a balance-transfer fee both post to the account in the same cycle.
requirements.when: Verify whether each fee type itself begins accruing interest (i.e., is added to the interest-bearing balance) as designed, per the cardholder agreement's specific terms for that fee type.
requirements.then: each fee type's interest-bearing status is an explicit, disclosed, and consistently-applied design decision (e.g., balance-transfer fee accrues interest as part of the BT balance; late fee does not accrue further interest) — never accidental or inconsistent between similar fee types.
requirements.failureMode: one fee type compounds interest while a functionally similar fee type doesn't, with no documented rate-engine rule driving the difference — an artifact of whichever engineer built that fee type's integration, not a deliberate rate policy.

requirements.title: Independently-launched promotional rate campaigns overlapping on the same customer
requirements.given: Retention team launches a targeted 3.99% APR retention offer to a customer segment; unaware, marketing separately launches a broad 0% seasonal purchase promo overlapping the same segment.
requirements.when: Simulate a customer who qualifies for both offers simultaneously, issued by two different, uncoordinated systems/teams.
requirements.then: rate engine detects the conflict at write-time (not read-time) and applies a single defined precedence rule, logging which offer was suppressed and why.
requirements.failureMode: both offers write independently to the account's rate record with no conflict detection between them, so the effective rate silently depends on which campaign's batch job ran last — not on any actual business precedence rule.
requirements.blockedOn: promo periods with start and end dates

requirements.title: Stored APR value matches disclosed/displayed precision exactly (no float drift)
requirements.given: APR is configured and stored as 24.99%.
requirements.when: Inspect the raw stored numeric value used by the interest-calculation engine (not just what's rendered on a statement or UI).
requirements.then: stored value is exact (e.g., a fixed-point/decimal type storing 0.2499), matching the disclosed 24.99% precisely, with no floating-point representation error entering the calculation.
requirements.failureMode: aPR is stored as a binary floating-point number (e.g., resulting in something like 0.24990000000000002 or 0.249899999999999996 after arithmetic), which renders correctly as '24.99%' in every display layer while the actual calculation silently uses a slightly different rate — a discrepancy invisible to manual QA that only reads formatted output.

requirements.title: Historical rate-in-effect-on-date is preserved and queryable after account/portfolio migration
requirements.given: Account is migrated from a legacy core processing system (e.g., after a portfolio acquisition) to the current system.
requirements.when: After migration, query 'what APR was in effect on [a date 8 months before migration]' for the migrated account.
requirements.then: full rate history (including promo start/end dates, penalty APR periods, and override history) migrates intact and is queryable exactly as it would be for a native account.
requirements.failureMode: migration only carries forward the CURRENT rate as of migration date, discarding rate history — so any later dispute, payoff-quote-for-a-past-date, or regulatory examination request for a pre-migration date cannot be accurately answered.
requirements.blockedOn: account lifecycle dates and product conversion

requirements.title: Any 45-day-notice rate increase triggers the periodic review obligation
requirements.given: A discretionary APR increase (based on credit risk or market conditions, not just delinquency) is applied and required a 45-day advance notice under 1026.9(c)(2).
requirements.when: Verify the account is automatically flagged for the ongoing periodic-review obligation the moment the qualifying increase takes effect.
requirements.then: every account with a qualifying rate increase enters the review queue automatically and completely — the review population is not limited to only delinquency-triggered increases.
requirements.failureMode: system only tracks review obligations for penalty-APR/delinquency increases (the narrower, more obvious case) and never flags discretionary risk-based or market-based increases for the broader §1026.59 review — reproducing the actual root cause class of the Citibank enforcement action.

requirements.title: First review occurs within the correct deadline, with the delinquency carve-out timing applied correctly
requirements.given: One account has a discretionary rate increase; a second account has a rate increase specifically under 1026.55(b)(4) for a payment 60+ days late.
requirements.when: Compute the deadline for the first required review for each account.
requirements.then: general account: first review no later than 6 months after the increase's effective date. Delinquency-triggered account: first review is not required until no later than 6 months after the sixth payment due date following the increase's effective date (a materially later, distinct deadline).
requirements.failureMode: system applies a single uniform 'first review' deadline formula to both account types, either reviewing the delinquency account too early (wasted review before behavior can be assessed) or reviewing the discretionary-increase account too late (a compliance violation).

requirements.title: Reviews continue at least every 6 months, not just once
requirements.given: An account underwent its first required §1026.59 review 6 months ago and did not qualify for a rate reduction at that time.
requirements.when: Advance another 6 months with no further manual action and check whether a second review automatically occurs.
requirements.then: a new review automatically triggers at least every 6 months on an ongoing basis until a valid termination condition is met — this is a recurring obligation, not a one-time event.
requirements.failureMode: system treats the §1026.59 obligation as satisfied after a single review and never re-triggers it, silently dropping accounts out of ongoing compliance after their first review cycle.
requirements.blockedOn: scheduled review engine and review dates

requirements.title: Review population includes every eligible account, with no silent exclusions
requirements.given: A cohort of 100,000 accounts had qualifying rate increases in the same period.
requirements.when: Run the review-population query and independently verify the count against the full set of accounts that actually had a qualifying increase.
requirements.then: 100% of eligible accounts appear in the review population — CFPB examinations have specifically found issuers 'inadvertently' failing to include all eligible accounts due to query/segmentation bugs.
requirements.failureMode: a subset of accounts is silently excluded from the review population due to a filter bug (e.g., accounts that also had an unrelated account status change, or accounts on a particular product code, being inadvertently dropped from the query).

requirements.title: Review uses the correct factor set, without conflating original-increase factors and current-new-account factors
requirements.given: Issuer's policy is to review using EITHER (a) the same factors that originally justified the increase, or (b) the factors currently used for pricing new accounts — a defined, documented choice.
requirements.when: Verify the review engine consistently applies only the chosen methodology, not a mix of both.
requirements.then: one consistent, documented methodology is applied to every review, matching what's disclosed in the issuer's own policies and procedures.
requirements.failureMode: system blends factors from both methodologies inconsistently across different accounts or review cycles — the specific error CFPB examiners found ('conflated re-evaluation factors') — producing indefensible, inconsistent outcomes across similar accounts.

requirements.title: Review criteria never exceed what Reg Z permits
requirements.given: Issuer's review logic includes an additional internal criterion (e.g., a minimum current credit score, or absence of the increase on any other account) not found in 1026.59(d)'s permitted factors.
requirements.when: Audit the review engine's actual decision logic against the specific factors 1026.59(d) allows.
requirements.then: only permitted factors are used to determine whether/how much to reduce the rate.
requirements.failureMode: system has accreted extra disqualifying criteria over time (often added for risk-management reasons unrelated to the regulation) that improperly prevent otherwise-qualifying accounts from receiving a required rate reduction — the second specific error class CFPB examiners identified.
requirements.blockedOn: scheduled review engine and review dates

requirements.title: Approved rate reduction is applied within 45 days of completing the evaluation
requirements.given: A review determines an account qualifies for a rate reduction.
requirements.when: Measure the elapsed time between the evaluation's completion date and the effective date of the resulting rate reduction.
requirements.then: rate reduction takes effect no later than 45 days after the evaluation was completed.
requirements.failureMode: evaluation completes promptly but the resulting rate change sits in a queue and doesn't actually take effect on the account until well past the 45-day requirement, due to a downstream batch-processing lag.

requirements.title: Rate reduction amount is defensibly tied to the review factors, not a blind full reversion or a token minimal decrease
requirements.given: An account's rate was increased from 15.99% to 23.99% for a payment 5 days late; 6 months of on-time payments follow and a review is performed.
requirements.when: Verify the resulting rate reduction (if any) is a reasoned output of the issuer's documented policy applied to the review factors — not a hardcoded full reversion to 15.99%, and not a token reduction designed to appear compliant while remaining punitive.
requirements.then: system is not required to revert to the original pre-increase rate, but whatever reduction is applied must be traceable to the actual review factors and the issuer's documented, reasonable policy — with the reasoning logged for examination.
requirements.failureMode: system either always fully reverts (potentially over-crediting in cases where partial reduction was actually warranted) or always applies the same negligible token reduction regardless of the review outcome, with no factor-driven reasoning behind the number.

requirements.title: Acquired-portfolio accounts get the correct special review treatment
requirements.given: Issuer acquires a portfolio of credit card accounts from another institution, some of which already carry increased rates from the prior owner.
requirements.when: Verify the review obligation logic for these accounts within 6 months of acquisition.
requirements.then: if the issuer reviews all acquired accounts within 6 months using its own new-account pricing factors, it is only required to continue §1026.59 reviews for rate increases that result from that acquisition review — not for every pre-acquisition increase indefinitely.
requirements.failureMode: system either ignores the acquired accounts' rate-increase history entirely (a gap that lets an old, never-reviewed penalty rate persist indefinitely) or incorrectly imposes the full ongoing review burden using the prior owner's original increase factors, which the issuer has no ability to evaluate.
requirements.blockedOn: scheduled review engine and review dates

requirements.title: Termination of the review obligation is correctly detected, neither early nor late
requirements.given: An account's increased-rate obligation should terminate under a specific enumerated condition (e.g., the rate is reduced to a level that is no longer subject to review, or the account is closed).
requirements.when: Simulate each enumerated termination condition and verify the review obligation stops exactly when a valid condition is met, and continues otherwise.
requirements.then: review obligation terminates only upon an actual enumerated condition, logged and auditable.
requirements.failureMode: system either keeps reviewing accounts indefinitely past a valid termination trigger (wasted operational cost, though not itself a violation) or — more seriously — stops reviewing an account based on an unrecognized/invalid condition, silently dropping a still-obligated account out of compliance.

requirements.title: Reduced rate does not exceed the higher of the consumer's pre-default rate or the lowest current acquisition rate
requirements.driver: CFPB Supervisory Highlights, Fall 2022 (Issue 28) — named credit card account management examination finding
requirements.given: A penalty-rate account undergoes its required §1026.59 review and is determined to warrant a rate reduction.
requirements.when: Verify the reduced rate is capped at (does not exceed) the higher of: (a) the APR that applied to the consumer's account before the penalty rate was imposed, or (b) the lowest APR currently offered to new customers for similar accounts.
requirements.then: the system enforces this specific ceiling on the reduced rate — a precise numeric floor requirement named directly in CFPB examination findings against real issuers who failed to apply it.
requirements.failureMode: system reduces the rate to some other value (e.g., a fixed percentage reduction, or a value from an unrelated internal table) that doesn't reference either the consumer's own pre-default rate or the current acquisition-rate floor, resulting in a reduction that is smaller than legally required.
requirements.blockedOn: product configuration and disclosed rate ranges

requirements.title: Rate re-evaluation factors reflect currently-applicable parameters, not stale historical ones
requirements.driver: CFPB Supervisory Highlights, Spring 2022 (Issue 26) — named credit card account management examination finding
requirements.given: A creditor's rate re-evaluation methodology references a 'minimum rate' or similar parameter that applied to the account's product/segment historically but has since been discontinued or changed.
requirements.when: Verify the re-evaluation calculation uses the parameter values that are actually applicable to the account AT THE TIME OF THE REVIEW, not values that were correct historically but are stale at review time.
requirements.then: re-evaluation logic pulls current, live parameter values at calculation time, with no hardcoded or cached historical constants that could silently go stale as the product's parameters change over time.
requirements.failureMode: re-evaluation calculation references a formerly-applicable minimum rate that no longer applies to the account, because the parameter was hardcoded or cached at some earlier point rather than looked up fresh — the exact, named root cause in a real CFPB examination finding against multiple creditors.
requirements.blockedOn: scheduled review engine and review dates

requirements.title: Full rate increase is evaluated for accounts converted from a fixed-rate structure
requirements.driver: CFPB Supervisory Highlights, Fall 2022 (Issue 28) — named credit card account management examination finding
requirements.given: An account that originally had a fixed (non-variable) APR is converted to a different rate structure (e.g., variable), and the conversion itself, or a subsequent change, constitutes a qualifying rate increase.
requirements.when: Verify the §1026.59 review evaluates the FULL rate increase experienced by the account since conversion, not merely the incremental change since the most recent review.
requirements.then: review logic correctly identifies and evaluates the complete rate increase relevant to a converted account, matching what CFPB examiners specifically found some issuers failing to do.
requirements.failureMode: system's review logic was built assuming accounts have always been on the current rate structure, so for fixed-to-variable converted accounts it only evaluates a partial slice of the actual increase — understating what the review should be assessing and potentially denying warranted reductions.
requirements.blockedOn: account lifecycle dates and product conversion

requirements.title: Review-date field in the system of record is accurately maintained, since it directly drives review-population inclusion
requirements.driver: CFPB Supervisory Highlights, Issue 26 (2022) — named credit card account management examination finding
requirements.given: An account's 'next review due' date field in the system of record is the mechanism that determines whether the account gets pulled into a given review cycle's population.
requirements.when: Verify this date field is set correctly and consistently at the time of the original rate increase and after every subsequent review, and audit for accounts where the field may be null, defaulted, or otherwise incorrect.
requirements.then: review-date field is populated accurately and reliably for every account with a qualifying rate increase, and the review-population query correctly captures every account whose review-date has arrived.
requirements.failureMode: a data-entry or system-integration defect leaves the review-date field blank, null, or incorrectly set for a subset of accounts, causing the review-population query to silently miss them — the specific, named root cause CFPB examiners identified as directly harming consumers who never received a rate-reduction evaluation they were owed.

requirements.title: MAPR is calculated per billing cycle for covered borrowers, distinct from standard APR
requirements.driver: Military Lending Act (10 U.S.C. § 987) / 32 CFR Part 232
requirements.given: A covered borrower (per DMDC database check) carries a credit card balance; the cycle includes standard interest plus a non-interest fee.
requirements.when: Compute the Military Annual Percentage Rate for that billing cycle, bundling in charges that Reg Z's standard APR/finance-charge definition would treat differently (e.g., certain fees TILA excludes but MLA includes).
requirements.then: mAPR is calculated fresh each billing cycle using the MLA's broader charge-inclusion rules, kept as a distinct value from the account's disclosed TILA APR.
requirements.failureMode: system reuses the standard TILA APR calculation (or a cached prior MAPR value) instead of recalculating MAPR per cycle with the correct MLA-specific charge inclusions, silently permitting an over-cap rate for a covered borrower.

requirements.title: 36% MAPR cap enforced as a hard ceiling for covered borrowers
requirements.given: Computed MAPR for a covered borrower's account would exceed 36% for the cycle given current interest and included fees.
requirements.when: Run the MAPR calculation and check the enforcement action taken.
requirements.then: system caps charges/fees for that cycle (or waives excess fees) so the effective MAPR does not exceed 36%, and flags the account for review.
requirements.failureMode: system calculates a MAPR above 36% and takes no corrective action, either charging the full amount or failing to flag the violation for compliance review.

requirements.title: No fee/charge is imposed in a billing cycle with no balance to calculate MAPR against, except the permitted participation fee
requirements.given: A covered borrower's account has a zero balance for an entire billing cycle (no MAPR can be meaningfully calculated).
requirements.when: Check whether any fee posts to the account for that cycle.
requirements.then: no fee is imposed for that cycle, with the specific exception that a participation fee may still be charged if it does not exceed $100 for the year.
requirements.failureMode: system imposes an annual fee, maintenance fee, or other charge during a zero-balance cycle for a covered borrower, or allows a participation fee above the $100 threshold.

requirements.title: A single non-bona-fide fee pulls every fee in that cycle into the MAPR calculation
requirements.given: A covered borrower's account has several fees in one cycle; the issuer classifies most as excludable 'bona fide' fees except one which does not meet the bona fide test.
requirements.when: Compute the MAPR for that cycle including the disputed fee.
requirements.then: because one fee fails the bona-fide test, ALL fees (both the disputed one and the otherwise-excludable bona fide ones) must be included in that cycle's MAPR calculation — the presence of one non-bona-fide fee taints the whole set.
requirements.failureMode: system evaluates each fee's bona-fide status independently and only includes the one non-bona-fide fee in the MAPR calculation, incorrectly continuing to exclude the otherwise-bona-fide fees and understating the true MAPR.

requirements.title: Covered-borrower status is checked at the correct times, not just once at origination
requirements.driver: Military Lending Act (10 U.S.C. § 987) / 32 CFR 232.5 (safe harbor)
requirements.given: A cardholder was not a covered borrower (no active-duty/dependent status) at account opening but later becomes one, or vice versa.
requirements.when: Verify when the system re-checks covered-borrower status against the DoD database relative to rate changes and new transactions.
requirements.then: coverage status is checked consistent with the issuer's documented safe-harbor timing (commonly at account opening and at defined trigger points such as credit-line increases), and the MAPR cap is applied/removed accordingly as status changes are detected.
requirements.failureMode: system checks covered-borrower status only once, at account opening, and never re-evaluates it — permanently misclassifying an account whose status has since changed in either direction.

requirements.title: MLA-covered population is correctly distinguished from the narrower SCRA-covered population
requirements.driver: Military Lending Act vs. SCRA — distinct populations and caps
requirements.given: An account holder is a covered borrower's dependent (MLA-covered) but is not personally on active duty (not SCRA-eligible in their own right).
requirements.when: Verify the system applies the 36% MAPR cap (MLA) to this account without incorrectly also applying, or incorrectly denying, the 6% SCRA cap which requires the account holder's own active-duty status.
requirements.then: each protection is evaluated against its own correct eligibility population and applied independently and correctly — MLA and SCRA are not interchangeable despite both being military rate protections.
requirements.failureMode: system has a single 'military protection' flag conflating MLA and SCRA eligibility, either wrongly extending the deeper 6% SCRA cap to an MLA-only dependent, or wrongly denying the 36% MLA cap because the account holder doesn't meet the narrower SCRA definition.

requirements.title: MLA and SCRA caps do not conflict when a borrower qualifies for both
requirements.given: An active-duty servicemember qualifies for both the SCRA's 6% cap (pre-service debt) and would separately be MLA-covered (36% MAPR ceiling) on the same account.
requirements.when: Compute the applicable rate/charge ceiling.
requirements.then: the more protective (lower) cap applies — here, SCRA's 6% governs since it's stricter than MLA's 36% — with the system correctly recognizing this isn't a conflict but a 'most protective standard applies' situation.
requirements.failureMode: system has competing, uncoordinated logic for each protection and applies whichever was evaluated last, rather than deterministically resolving to the lower of the two caps.
requirements.blockedOn: product configuration and disclosed rate ranges

requirements.title: System can execute the MLA's void-contract/refund-all-interest remedy for a confirmed violation
requirements.driver: Military Lending Act (10 U.S.C. § 987) — void-contract remedy; CFPB v. online lender (S.D.N.Y., filed Sept. 29, 2022) alleging MAPR exceeded 36% via interest plus membership fees
requirements.given: A confirmed MLA violation is identified for a covered borrower's account (e.g., MAPR exceeded 36% through a combination of interest and a monthly fee that pushed the effective rate over the cap — a real litigated fact pattern in prior CFPB MLA enforcement actions).
requirements.when: Verify the system's remediation tooling can execute the legal remedy: the credit agreement is voidable from inception for the violation period, meaning the borrower owes principal but no interest is chargeable, and any interest already collected during the violation period must be identified and refunded.
requirements.then: remediation tooling can isolate the exact interest amounts charged during the violation period, zero them out prospectively, and calculate/issue the required refund for interest already collected — a specific, testable operational capability, not just a policy statement.
requirements.failureMode: system has no mechanism to distinguish 'interest that should never have been charged due to an MLA violation' from ordinary interest, making the legally-required remedy operationally impossible to execute accurately, or requiring an error-prone manual reconstruction.

requirements.title: Rate-exportation basis matches the actual chartered/located state of the issuing bank
requirements.driver: National Bank Act rate exportation; DIDMCA § 521 — legally unsettled, fact-intensive area; confirm with counsel
requirements.given: A card program relies on rate exportation (National Bank Act / DIDMCA) so that the issuing bank's home-state rate applies nationwide, including to residents of states with lower usury caps.
requirements.when: Verify the 'located' state used to justify the exported APR in the system's compliance records matches the bank-of-issue's actual charter/principal-office state as legally determined, not the marketing/program-manager partner's state or a state chosen for convenience.
requirements.then: the exported-rate justification is tied to and auditable against the actual issuing bank's legally relevant location, consistently, for every account relying on that exportation basis.
requirements.failureMode: system configuration ties the 'exported rate' justification to whichever entity's name is on the card face or marketing materials rather than the legally relevant chartered/located bank, creating exposure if the actual economic/lending relationship doesn't match the documented basis.

requirements.title: Colorado (or other DIDMCA opt-out state) residency correctly routes to the applicable rate regime
requirements.driver: DIDMCA § 525 state opt-out provision; Colorado opt-out — legally unsettled, fact-intensive area; confirm with counsel
requirements.given: Colorado opted out of DIDMCA rate exportation for state-chartered bank lending programs (the first new opt-out in decades); a card program's rate-exportation model may not apply the same way to Colorado residents as to residents of other states, depending on the specific program's bank charter type and structure.
requirements.when: Verify the system correctly identifies Colorado (and any other current opt-out states) residency and applies the program's own determined correct rate treatment for that state, rather than defaulting to the same exported rate used everywhere else.
requirements.then: colorado residency (or other applicable opt-out states) triggers the program's specifically determined, correct rate treatment — a deliberate, documented configuration, not an accidental default.
requirements.failureMode: system has a single nationwide rate-exportation configuration with no state-specific override capability, meaning a change in one state's opt-out status can't be operationally reflected without a full re-engineering effort — a real exposure given this is an active, evolving area of state legislation.
requirements.blockedOn: product configuration and disclosed rate ranges

requirements.title: Economic-interest and risk-retention records are internally consistent with the disclosed lender of record
requirements.driver: "True lender" doctrine (multi-factor / 'predominant economic interest' test) — legally unsettled, fact-intensive area; confirm with counsel
requirements.given: A card program is structured as a bank-fintech partnership, where a bank is the disclosed lender of record and a nonbank program manager markets, services, or has some economic interest in the receivables.
requirements.when: Verify the system's actual records of who funds the credit line, who bears credit-loss risk, and who retains the economic interest in the receivables are consistent with the disclosed lender-of-record structure — since 'true lender' analysis by courts and regulators turns on exactly these operational facts, not just contractual labels.
requirements.then: funding source, risk-retention percentages, and economic-interest allocation in the system's actual books and records match what's represented in customer disclosures and regulatory filings, with a clear, consistent audit trail.
requirements.failureMode: system/operational records (e.g., which entity's balance sheet actually funds new receivables day-to-day, or which entity absorbs losses) drift from the disclosed structure over time as the program evolves, creating a gap between the legal fiction and the operational reality that a true-lender challenge would specifically probe.
requirements.blockedOn: override expiry dates and authorisation records

requirements.title: APR terms on a receivable remain unaltered through sale/assignment to a nonbank purchaser
requirements.driver: "Valid when made" doctrine — legally unsettled, fact-intensive area; confirm with counsel
requirements.given: A pool of credit card receivables (with their originally-disclosed APRs) is sold or assigned from the originating bank to a nonbank purchaser, consistent with common securitization or portfolio-sale practice.
requirements.when: Verify the APR and other credit terms on each receivable remain exactly as validly originated at the time of sale/assignment, with no alteration, and that this is fully auditable.
requirements.then: system preserves an immutable record of each receivable's originally-disclosed, validly-made APR terms through any subsequent sale or assignment, consistent with the 'valid when made' doctrine's premise that a validly originated rate isn't rendered invalid merely by later assignment.
requirements.failureMode: a data migration or system-of-record handoff during a receivables sale silently normalizes or recalculates APRs to fit the acquiring system's rate table/precision, introducing discrepancies between the originally-disclosed rate and what's actually charged post-sale.

requirements.title: System can enforce a hard global APR ceiling across every product, tier, and balance type simultaneously
requirements.driver: S.381 / H.R.1944, 10 Percent Credit Card Interest Rate Cap Act (119th Congress) — introduced, pending in committee, not enacted
requirements.given: A hypothetical new federal statute imposes a flat maximum APR (e.g., 10%) applicable across all consumer credit card balances, superseding the account's normal tiered/risk-based/variable/penalty rate structure.
requirements.when: Verify the rate engine has (or could be configured with) a single global ceiling parameter that caps every APR calculation path — standard, promotional, penalty, variable, override — without requiring a separate code change to each individually.
requirements.then: a global ceiling can be applied centrally and takes effect across purchase, cash advance, balance transfer, penalty, and override rates simultaneously, on a specified effective date, without needing per-bucket manual reconfiguration that risks missing a rate type.
requirements.failureMode: rate ceiling logic (if any exists at all, e.g., for existing state usury exemptions) is scattered across multiple independent code paths per product/balance type, meaning a new global cap would require dozens of separate, error-prone changes under legislative time pressure rather than one central control.

requirements.title: A scheduled future sunset date correctly reverts rate-cap behavior without manual re-programming
requirements.driver: S.381 / H.R.1944 — proposed 5-year sunset provision, effective through Jan. 1, 2031; not enacted
requirements.given: The pending federal cap proposal includes a specific hardcoded sunset date (January 1, 2031) after which the cap would no longer apply by statute.
requirements.when: Verify the system supports scheduling a rate-regime change years in advance and correctly executes the reversion exactly on the specified date without requiring someone to remember to manually flip it off.
requirements.then: a future-dated regime change (cap start and cap sunset) can be configured once and will execute correctly and automatically on the specified calendar date, years later, consistent with how other date-triggered rate-structure changes are already handled elsewhere in the system.
requirements.failureMode: system has no concept of a far-future scheduled rate-regime change; implementing the cap would require an ad hoc manual process that also has no corresponding automated 'turn it back off' mechanism, creating real risk of the cap silently persisting past its legal sunset date (continuing to underprice risk) or being manually removed too early.
requirements.blockedOn: product configuration and disclosed rate ranges

requirements.title: Remediation tooling can support full interest forfeiture for a violation period, not just excess-above-cap refunds
requirements.driver: S.381 / H.R.1944 — proposed full-interest-forfeiture penalty for knowing violations; not enacted
requirements.given: The pending proposal's remedy for a knowing violation is forfeiture of the ENTIRE interest charged on the debt (not merely the amount above the 10% ceiling) — a materially harsher remedy structure than the MLA's void-contract-and-refund-excess approach.
requirements.when: Verify remediation tooling could, if ever needed, distinguish between 'refund the excess above a cap' (the MLA/SCRA pattern already tested) and 'forfeit all interest for the period' (a different, more severe calculation), and produce the correct one for the applicable remedy.
requirements.then: remediation logic explicitly supports both remedy types as distinct configurable calculations, since conflating them (e.g., only ever being able to compute an excess-refund) would understate what a full-forfeiture remedy legally requires if such a provision were ever enacted for any product.
requirements.failureMode: system's only existing remediation calculation is 'excess above a cap,' inherited from SCRA/MLA-style logic, with no way to compute or execute a full-forfeiture remedy — a gap that would surface at the worst possible time if a harsher remedy structure like this one were ever enacted.

requirements.title: System can enforce a fee limit defined relative to another calculated value, not just a flat dollar/percentage cap
requirements.driver: S.381 / H.R.1944 — proposed fee-limited-to-finance-charges provision; not enacted
requirements.given: The pending proposal would limit total fees to no more than the total finance charges (interest) actually assessed on the account — a cap that isn't a fixed number but is dynamically defined relative to a separately-calculated running total.
requirements.when: Verify the fee-assessment engine could, if required, check a proposed fee against a running total of finance charges already assessed for the relevant period, and block or reduce the fee if it would exceed that dynamically-computed ceiling.
requirements.then: fee engine supports conditional caps referencing another live calculated value (e.g., cumulative finance charges), not just static configured limits — a materially different and more complex capability than the flat-dollar safe-harbor caps the system already handles for late fees.
requirements.failureMode: every existing fee cap in the system is a static configured number; there is no mechanism to check a fee against a dynamically-changing reference value like 'total finance charges assessed to date,' which would require new engineering (not just configuration) if a fee-relative-to-interest cap were ever enacted for any product.
requirements.blockedOn: product configuration and disclosed rate ranges

requirements.title: Per-charge historical records are retained at sufficient granularity to support a private-right-of-action lookback period
requirements.driver: S.381 / H.R.1944 — proposed 2-year private-right-of-action window; not enacted
requirements.given: The pending proposal creates a private right of action allowing a consumer to recover interest/fees, with claims required to be brought within 2 years of a violation.
requirements.when: Verify the system retains per-transaction, per-charge historical detail (which rate applied, on which balance, on which date) at a granularity sufficient to reconstruct and defend against an individual claim covering at least the applicable lookback period, for any account.
requirements.then: historical rate/charge detail is retained and retrievable at the individual-transaction level for at least the relevant lookback period, supporting both proactive compliance review and defense against individual claims.
requirements.failureMode: system retains only aggregated monthly totals rather than per-transaction rate/charge detail beyond a short retention window, making it operationally impossible to reconstruct exactly what rate was applied to which specific balance on which specific date if a claim were filed close to the lookback deadline.
